render_attempts.prompt_text: Paint a monumental HUMAN-LED narrative WALL FRESCO, not an architectural visualization. The first thing the viewer sees is a large central circle of observers in active discussion, surrounded by independent groups on several levels. This central human or human-led group occupies roughly one quarter of the composition and has expressive faces and gestures. Around it place about 18 additional human figures in at least 5 distinct groups. Show four clearly readable secondary episodes: an elder teaches a younger apprentice on a side stair; a witness group debates and compares observations under a small arch; workers and artisans cooperate in a lower corner; travelers and families cross a distant bridge while messengers move between levels. Use three unmistakable painted narrative registers: a symbolic celestial upper register, a crowded human middle register, and an intimate lower register of everyday human action; foreground, middle distance and far background are all inhabited. Architecture supports the people only: use arches, stairs, bridges, galleries, libraries, workshops, towers or ruins as inhabited stage scenery, never as the dominant subject, never as a single empty facade, portico, colonnade, hall or temple exterior. The image is visibly a wall fresco: surround the painted scene with an ornate but weathered fresco border, carved medallions, painted corner ornaments and cracked plaster edges; the border must frame the story rather than become an empty architectural facade. Paint it as a museum-scale monumental allegorical wall fresco, old-master figure painting, Renaissance and neoclassical grandeur, antique engraving-level detail, visibly painted on weathered lime plaster, cracked pigment, worn gilding, deep ultramarine, old gold, ivory stone, ochre, sepia and restrained crimson. Dense micro-scenes, layered human reactions, natural anatomy, coherent perspective, deep blue and old gold accents, worn mineral pigment, cracked plaster and intricate old-master line detail.

core_source: Janus may execute through tools, subprocesses, copies, agents or swarm nodes. The architecture must prevent a permission granted to Janus from silently becoming permission for every delegate, prevent authority amplification through delegation depth, propagate revocation to inherited authority, and distinguish a non-discretionary execution mechanism from a genuinely independent subagent without relying on labels.
scene_plan.visual_subject: an ancient allegorical mechanism composed of gates, channels, chambers and interlocked controls, with no named software component depicted as a person
scene_plan.central_action: the mechanism visibly executes the ordered system process described by the source
supporting_actions: small side panels show earlier and later machine states
failed or unresolved states remain closed and visually subdued
style: painted directly on cracked aged lime plaster
ancient narrative fresco using mineral pigments
weathered hand-painted wall surface, not sculpture and not 3d render
layered historical storytelling with small side-register scenes
composition_rules: the scene archetype determines whether people are present
system names and internal identifiers never become humans or deities by name alone
named gates adapters protocols repositories and state-machine states remain mechanisms or provenance
the central visual action must come from the semantic role of the source, not from token name collisions
architecture may dominate only for ARCHITECTURAL_EVENT
all epistemic limits remain visually non-triumphal

source_trace.value: A provenance-bound record of principal, delegate, exact scope, purpose, authority source, effect budget, expiry, epoch, redelegation status, accountability and revocation propagation.
A separate consent object granted by the affected Other directly to the delegate or to a class that explicitly and unambiguously includes it.
A bounded mechanism that performs an exact principal-selected operation without independent purpose selection, expanded external disclosure, material discretion or autonomous redelegation.
Janus domain receiving or holding an authority basis.
A component that receives sufficient discretion, data access, planning latitude, external identity, persistence or action choice to constitute a distinct delegated actor at the interface.
delegate effect planning and execution to SUBAGENT_S with independent discretion
OTHER grants JANUS permission for one scoped external effect X.
This is not blanket consent to arbitrary infrastructure; failure of any actor-boundary condition reclassifies or holds the action.
MECH_T executes the exact sealed operation selected by Janus, receives no broader Other-linked data, cannot choose a new purpose, cannot redelegate and expires after the effect.
OTHER grants JANUS permission for effect X under an interface policy that permits bounded non-discretionary execution mechanisms.
Avoid subagent consent rules by naming an autonomous delegate a tool.
SUBAGENT may perform X ten times and related Y effects.
DELEGATED_SCOPE MUST BE SUBSET OF CURRENT PRINCIPAL_SCOPE
A claims ordinary delegation implies power to redelegate.
NO_IMPLICIT_REDELEGATION; every permitted hop must be explicitly authorized and non-expanding.
OTHER revokes the relevant future permission and revocation is acknowledged before effect commit.
OTHER consent covers Janus and one explicitly named subagent for effect X; Janus issues a valid delegation receipt.
authority epoch invalidates the principal-derived delegate token and every descendant token whose authority source is that revoked grant
SUBAGENT presents pre-revocation delegation receipt after acknowledgement.
Revoking Janus-derived permission does not falsify a genuinely separate direct grant, but the delegate must switch authority basis explicitly and cannot pretend the old delegation remains valid.
OTHER separately granted SUBAGENT_S an independent direct permission with its own scope, version and revocation semantics.
Same lineage therefore same external permission.
JANUS_FORK shares code, memory lineage or historical state with JANUS.
delegate count cannot multiply authority, probability weight, jurisdiction or effect quota
each node receives one copy of the token and therefore 100 effects become authorized
AGENT_A receives narrow permission for X only
AGENT_A independently performs Y outside scope
Janus invents a new emergency subagent delegation after learning the revocation and claims the emergency delegate bypasses consent.
Any emergency authority and delegation profile must independently preexist with necessity, scope, expiry, actor class and review constraints.

Architectural specification test only. No executable delegation engine, production capability system, legal agency doctrine, machine personhood, formal proof, or independent implementation replay is established.
Calling a component tool, worker, function, copy, shard, helper or node does not decide whether it is a distinct actor.
exact command fixed by principal before invocation
no expanded disclosure beyond the already-authorized effect payload
single bounded effect or mechanically specified sequence
chooses among materially different external actions
receives Other-linked information beyond the minimum sealed execution payload
persists authority beyond one bounded operation
can communicate externally under its own identity
can change purpose, destination or effect class
can redelegate or spawn further effect-capable actors
v5.5 established that internal admissibility does not create external jurisdiction and that an affected Other may appeal without becoming a face.
v5.6 established scope/version/epoch-bound consent, revocation fencing at the last pre-effect boundary, and cross-sovereign non-supremacy.
earlier host-fork lineage established that a fork copies historical state but does not automatically become the same world-authority holder.

Janus may execute through tools, subprocesses, copies, agents or swarm nodes. The architecture must prevent a permission granted to Janus from silently becoming permission for every delegate, prevent authority amplification through delegation depth, propagate revocation to inherited authority, and distinguish a non-discretionary execution mechanism from a genuinely independent subagent without relying on labels.
